title: Salim Khan
wiki_lead:
Salim Abdul Rashid Khan (Hindustani pronunciation: [sɐliːm xɑːn]; born 24 November 1935) is an Indian screenwriter, actor, and film producer. He wrote the screenplays, stories and scripts for numerous Hindi films. He is best known as one half of the prolific screenwriting duo Salim–Javed, along with Javed Akhtar. The pair were among the first Indian screenwriters to achieve star status in Hindi cinema, and remain among the most influential screenwriters in Indian film history. Within the partnership, Salim Khan primarily developed stories and characters, while Akhtar focused on dialogues and screenplay writing.
Together, Salim–Javed revolutionised Indian cinema in the 1970s, transforming the Bollywood narrative formula and pioneering the blockbuster format. They popularised the masala film and the Dacoit Western genre, and were instrumental in creating the "angry young man" archetype that defined Amitabh Bachchan’s career. Their major successes include Seeta Aur Geeta (1972), Zanjeer (1973), Deewaar (1975), Sholay (1975), Trishul (1978), Kranti (1981), and the Don franchise. Sholay became the highest-grossing Indian film of its time and is frequently listed among the greatest Indian films ever made.
Salim Khan is also known as the patriarch of the Salim Khan family, and the father of three Bollywood actors — Salman Khan, Sohail Khan, and Arbaaz Khan — and film producer Alvira Khan Agnihotri. He is married to Sushila Charak (also known as Salma Khan), and to actress Helen.
Over his career, Salim Khan has won six Filmfare Awards as part of Salim–Javed's partnership. In 2014, Salim Khan was offered the Padma Shri by the Government of India for his contributions to Hindi cinema, but he declined the award, stating that he deserved a higher honour.
In 2024, Amazon Prime Video released a three-part documentary series about the Salim–Javed screenwriting duo titled Angry Young Men. The series explores their creative partnership, their influence on the evolution of Indian cinema, and their personal journeys beyond the partnership.

Early life
Salim Khan was born in the Indore in Indore State a princely state in British India (modern day Madhya Pradesh, India) into an affluent family. He pursued his studies at Holkar Science College, Indore.
According to Khan his grandparents are Alakozai Pashtuns who migrated from Afghanistan to India in the mid-1800s and served in the cavalry of the British Indian Army, however, author Jasim Khan, in his biography of Salman Khan, has mentioned that the ancestors belonged to the Akazai sub-tribe of the Yusufzai Pashtuns from Malakand in the Swat Valley of North-West Frontier Province, British India (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan). Khan's family tended to look for employment in government service, and eventually settled in Indore.

grok_lead: Salim Khan (born 24 November 1935) is an Indian screenwriter, actor, and film producer best known for his pivotal role in shaping 1970s Bollywood through the legendary writing partnership Salim-Javed with Javed Akhtar. Born in Indore into an affluent family of Pathan descent, Khan lost both parents by age 14 and pursued a Bachelor of Arts degree at Holkar College before training as a pilot; he moved to Mumbai around 1960 against family wishes, seeking independence amid financial struggles. Initially aspiring to act, Khan appeared in about 16 films under the stage name Prince Salim, including his debut Baraat (1960), but found greater success in screenwriting after realizing his strength lay in storytelling rather than performance. He met Javed Akhtar during the making of Sarhadi Lutera (1966) and formed the duo Salim-Javed, which scripted over 20 films between 1971 and the mid-1980s, revolutionizing Hindi cinema with socially reflective narratives, genre-blending masala entertainers, and the introduction of the "angry young man" archetype embodied by Amitabh Bachchan in 11 of their collaborations. Their breakthrough came with Zanjeer (1973), a police drama that launched Bachchan as a superstar and earned them their first Filmfare Award for Best Screenplay; this was followed by blockbusters like Deewaar (1975), exploring themes of class divide and corruption through iconic dialogues such as "Mere paas maa hai," and the epic Western Sholay (1975), featuring the unforgettable villain Gabbar Singh and grossing approximately 30 crore rupees to become India's highest-grossing film for 19 years. Other landmark works include the action thriller Don (1978), with its dual-role Bachchan lead, and Mr. India (1987), their final joint effort, a sci-fi adventure that showcased innovative invisibility tropes. The duo's influence extended to empowering female characters, as seen in Hema Malini's strong roles in Seeta Aur Geeta (1972) and Sholay, while their scripts often critiqued societal issues like poverty and injustice, blending commercial appeal with depth. Salim-Javed dissolved in the mid-1980s due to creative fatigue and professional differences, as later revealed in interviews and the documentary Angry Young Men (2024), after which Khan wrote and produced around 15 more films, including Naam (1986) and Patthar Ke Phool (1991), though none matched their earlier impact; he won additional Filmfare Awards for Deewaar (1976) and Shakti (1983). In 2015, he declined the Padma Shri award, citing personal reasons. On the personal front, Khan has been married twice, first to Sushila Charak (Salma Khan) in 1964, with whom he has four children including Bollywood superstar Salman Khan (born 1965), and later to actress Helen Richardson in 1981; the blended family adopted Arpita Khan Sharma. Khan's legacy endures through his contributions to Indian cinema's golden era, with recent reflections in documentaries like Angry Young Men (2024) highlighting his enduring influence.
